claims.text: Adding approximately 0.1 at.% yttrium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The yttrium addition promotes formation of an adherent, slow-growing, yttria-enriched oxide scale.
The untreated alloy has a non-adherent or rapidly growing oxide scale under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
The relevant structural mediator is a yttria-enriched oxide scale at the metal-oxide interface.
Yttrium segregates to oxide grain boundaries.
Yttrium segregates to the metal-oxide interface.
Segregated yttrium promotes nucleation of a stable, adherent, yttria-rich layer.
The yttria-rich layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Reduced oxygen diffusion decreases the high-temperature oxidation rate.
At 1000°C in flowing air for 100 hours, the yttrium-treated alloy will gain less weight than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified exposure conditions, the yttrium-treated alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified exposure conditions, the yttrium-treated alloy will have higher oxidation resistance than the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy exhibits faster oxidation kinetics at 1000°C in air over 100 hours.
The untreated alloy forms a less protective oxide scale at 1000°C in air over 100 hours.
The expected improvement is bounded to approximately atmospheric-pressure air, 1000°C, and exposure durations near 100 hours.
The effect may differ substantially at other temperatures, pressures, or in other reactive atmospheres.
The optimal yttrium concentration may involve a trade-off between oxidation resistance and embrittlement.
